source.title: More Than a Toy: Random Matrix Models Predict How Real-World Neural Representations Generalize
source.authors: Alexander Wei; Wei Hu; Jacob Steinhardt

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. No material garbling or cutoff is apparent.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures training and generalization risk for ridge regression on neural representations from natural image datasets, extending the study of generalization gaps to this setting. It does not test the specific versions listed.
record.gate_note: The paper reports predictor-to-generalization-risk correlations in Table 2 and describes cases where empirical risk is a poor proxy for test risk. Cited findings from other work are not recorded as rows. Its results do not measure any of the specific behaviors named in V1–V8.
record.test_reason: The study evaluates risk predictors for ridge regression on fixed neural representations. It does not test V1–V8: natural-label interpolation alone does not establish V1, sample-size scaling does not test width scaling, and norm-based risk prediction without sharpness measurements does not test V7.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate. The authors find that GCV accurately predicts ridge-regression risk on realistic neural representations, prove convergence under a local random matrix hypothesis, and explain pretraining benefits and sample-size scaling through alignment together with eigendecay. Their conclusions concern this regression setting; extension beyond it remains a proposed direction.
record.recipe_differences: The experiments use kernel ridge regression on empirical neural tangent kernel representations, not standard gradient training of networks to fit labels. The paper also compares GCV with norm- and spectrum-based risk predictors.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset and representation setting affect the reported performance of the spectrum-only and norm-based predictors; Flowers-102 has no scaling experiment because it consists of 2040 images.

fits_no_version.finding: Across the five Table 2 configurations, GCV correlations with generalization risk are 0.996, 0.999, 0.996, 0.999, and 0.979. Spectrum-only correlations range from 0.080 to 0.977; norm-based correlations are negative.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For ridge regression on the tested fixed neural representations, GCV predicts generalization risk better than the tested norm-based and fitted spectrum-only predictors.

record.problems: The experiments concern ridge regression on fixed neural representations, not end-to-end standard gradient training or arbitrary-label memorization. The paper states that its full neural tangent kernel is approximated by a single-logit kernel repeated across outputs. No uncertainty estimates are reported for the Table 2 correlations.
record.rows_left_out: Not applicable; 15 Table 2 correlation results are recorded. Other plotted risk curves and cited prior-work results were not extracted as additional rows.

untested.parts: Matched random-label and natural-label training, including random-label held-out performance.
Width increases beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected training and the role of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizers under limited or broader tuning.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adapted training recipes.
Dropout interventions, training-set-size dependence, and joint removal with weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, its association with generalization gaps, and comparisons against norm- and margin-based rankings.
Removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: The extracted Table 2 heading order is misleading: the all-1.000 correlation column belongs to ground truth. Its scaling slopes also match the actual rates reported elsewhere, confirming the GCV/ground-truth column correction. All recorded rows evaluate predictors and belong under fits_no_version.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label held-out accuracy under the same architecture and training recipe.
Width sweeps past the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under varying tuning and regularization choices.
Large versus small batches under fixed epoch budgets and adapted recipes.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its comparison with norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring the resulting test-accuracy change.
